posts.post_text: We banned ChatGPT in our analytics department last month. Not because AI is bad — because nobody could explain where the numbers came from. When a regulator asks 'how did you arrive at this figure?' and the answer is 'GPT said so', you've got a compliance problem. The AI trust gap is real and growing.
posts.angle: High-value ICP prospects (VP Ops, COO, CEO) engaging on a compliance-driven AI trust post — validate the explainability problem from a builder's perspective, not a vendor's
posts.draft_comment: The 'GPT said so' answer is exactly where trust falls apart — and it's not even the regulator you should worry about first, it's the analyst who can't retrace their own work the next morning. We kept hearing the same thing when building Milo: people don't need more AI in their analytics, they need AI they can actually stand behind in a meeting. Funny how 'explainability' sounds like a technical problem until it's a careers problem. What does auditability even look like in practice at your org — is anyone actually solving it or just avoiding the tools?

posts.post_text: We spent 18 months building a Power BI dashboard that our finance team refuses to use. They still export everything to Excel and email it around. The building part was easy. Getting people to actually trust the numbers enough to quote them in a board meeting? That's the real challenge nobody talks about. Anyone else hit this wall?
posts.angle: ICP prospect COO at 140-person firm hitting the trust wall with Power BI — validate the exact pain point (board-meeting credibility, not tool adoption) and add the insight that this is a data trust problem not a dashboard problem
posts.draft_comment: The 'they just export to Excel anyway' story is so common it's basically a rite of passage at this point. But I think the real issue isn't adoption — it's that nobody's confident enough in where the numbers came from to stake their reputation on them in a room full of executives. A dashboard tells you what, it rarely tells you why you should believe it. Did your finance team ever articulate what it would actually take for them to trust it?

posts.post_text: Unpopular opinion: most operational dashboards are vanity projects. We had 47 KPIs on our ops dashboard. Nobody looked at it. Cut it to 5 metrics that actually drive decisions. Usage went from 10% to 85%. The problem with BI isn't the tools — it's that we measure everything and understand nothing.
posts.angle: ICP prospect (Director of Operations at Summit Group) engaging on dashboard bloat — validate the 47→5 insight, add the 'why 10% usage is actually the honest signal' layer
posts.draft_comment: 47 KPIs and 10% usage isn't a failure — it's your team telling you exactly what mattered. The hard part isn't cutting to 5, it's resisting the pressure to add the 6th when someone senior asks 'but what about procurement cycle time?' Most dashboards die by committee, one metric at a time. How did you hold the line on keeping it at 5?

posts.post_text: Hot take: self-service BI is a myth. We gave everyone Power BI licenses and what happened? 200 reports, zero consistency, three different definitions of 'revenue'. The promise of democratising data is great until you realise nobody agrees on what the data means. Build vs buy isn't the question — it's 'who owns the truth?'
posts.angle: ICP prospect (Innovation Director at NorthStar Retail) engaging with a post about self-service BI chaos — validate the 'who owns the truth' framing and add the insight that the problem isn't access to data, it's the absence of shared definitions baked into the tooling itself
posts.draft_comment: The 200 reports thing is so recognisable. Everyone's technically using the same tool but they're all building their own version of reality. The problem was never access — it was that nobody defined 'revenue' before they handed out the licenses. Who's supposed to own that conversation, the data team or the business?

posts.post_text: AI hallucinations in analytics are a security issue, not just an accuracy issue. If your AI tool generates a financial report with hallucinated numbers and someone makes a decision based on it, that's not a bug — it's a material risk. We need to start treating AI outputs with the same scrutiny as we treat user inputs.
posts.angle: CISO at a healthcare org framing hallucinations as a security risk — validate the framing, add the nuance that the real danger is misplaced trust not just wrong numbers, with ICP prospect Andrew Mills watching
posts.draft_comment: The framing here is right and I don't think it gets said enough. The hallucination itself isn't always the problem — it's that the output looks clean and confident, so nobody questions it before it moves upstream into a decision. User inputs get sanitised because people learned the hard way what happens when they don't. AI outputs haven't had that reckoning yet. Wonder how many finance or ops leaders have actually seen a hallucinated number make it into a board deck without anyone catching it.

posts.post_text: Had a fascinating conversation with a client yesterday. They spent £200k on a BI platform and the only person who can use it is the one who built it. Self-service my arse. The gap between what vendors promise and what actually happens in a 50-person company is enormous. When will the industry admit that most BI tools are built for data teams, not business teams?
posts.angle: CEO at 65-person firm calling out BI vendor hype, with a COO in the thread — validate the core truth with a specific observation about who these tools are actually designed for
posts.draft_comment: The £200k number stings but the real cost is the 49 people who just gave up and went back to spreadsheets. Most BI tools are architected around the person who builds the thing — the data model, the permissions, the whole mental model. Business teams don't think in tables and joins, they think in questions. And no vendor wants to admit their 'self-service' is just self-service for people who already know SQL.

posts.post_text: Just had our quarterly review and the CFO asked why the numbers in our BI dashboard don't match the numbers in the ERP. Turns out three different teams were applying different filters to the same dataset. AI won't fix this. Culture will. But nobody wants to hear that.
posts.angle: Commercial Director calling out a culture problem over a tooling problem — validate the diagnosis but add the nuance that tooling either enables or erodes the culture around data trust
posts.draft_comment: Three teams, three filters, one dataset — that's not a culture problem in isolation, that's what happens when the tool makes it too easy to go rogue without anyone knowing. Culture sets the intention, but the system has to make the right behaviour the path of least resistance. How many of those filter decisions were deliberate, and how many were just people not realising anyone else was looking at the same numbers?

posts.post_text: Rolled out Copilot to 500 users last quarter. Usage after 90 days? 12%. The problem isn't the tool — it's that nobody knows what to ask it. We're essentially paying for a very expensive autocomplete. Shadow AI is the real story here — people are using ChatGPT on their phones because Copilot is too locked down.
posts.angle: IT Director surfacing real adoption failure and shadow AI problem — validate the 12% finding as a systemic insight, not a Copilot-specific one
posts.draft_comment: That 12% number is brutal but I'd bet it shows up almost identically across most enterprise AI rollouts right now. The shadow AI point is the real tell — people aren't lazy, they're just going where the friction is lowest and the answers feel useful. The question nobody wants to answer is: what does it actually mean to 'know what to ask' when the data underneath is still a mess?
